A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TCAP research. Their complete main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original backdoor-defense experiments across three MLLMs and five datasets, including detection results, component ablations, and sensitivity analyses in Tables 1–4 and 6–9.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experimental results in Tables 1–4 and 6–9, including visual and textual attack evaluations and appendix sensitivity analyses.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same attention decomposition, adaptive GMM fitting, head selection, Dawid–Skene vote aggregation, sample filtering, and retraining procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ScienceQA, PhD, DocVQA, Recap-COCO, and SEED-Bench. The five visual attack types and the ScienceQA prefix and PhD HiddenKiller textual scenarios are unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Vanilla FT, Random Drop, SampDetox, and BYE as comparators; Table 2 retains BYE. Updated citation years do not change comparator identity or participation.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 and Appendix A retain the same model configurations, dataset sample counts, metrics, default 10% poisoning rate, target output, and training settings. The appendix parameter sweeps also use unchanged settings.

E4.justification: The joint attention visualization, four component ablations, textual-trigger tests, and poison-rate, layer-count, head-count, and voting-threshold analyses are unchanged in Figure 3, Tables 3–4, and Appendix B.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same point estimates without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. No uncertainty-reporting practice is added or revised.

E6.justification: All numerical results in Tables 1–4 and 6–9 match, as do the plotted findings in Figure 3. For example, TCAP on Qwen3-VL with DocVQA retains CP 90.57 and ASR 0.33 in Table 1.

T1.justification: The loss definitions, attention-entropy reasoning, allocation vectors, GMM formulation, separation score, and voting equations remain unchanged in Equations 1–10. Revising the Akaike citation year does not alter the mathematical content.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims of a universal, modality-agnostic attention-allocation fingerprint and an unsupervised defense with strong robustness and preserved clean performance.

C2.justification: The explanations of complementary attention anomalies, BYE's limitations, and TCAP's parameter sensitivity are unchanged in Sections 3.3 and 5 and Appendices B–C. No substantive limitation or applicability qualification is added.

D1.justification: The repository link and technical disclosures are unchanged. Appendix A.3 retains four A100 GPUs, five training epochs, batch size 16, model-specific learning rates, and the same TCAP hyperparameters; Appendices D–E retain the decomposition details and algorithm.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning remain the same. Bibliographic changes update publication information, author details, titles, and citation years for existing works rather than introducing new literature or comparisons.

P1.justification: v2 adds a third affiliation and a funding acknowledgement, replaces the preprint notice with conference publication details, and standardizes bibliography entries and some punctuation. The scientific narrative and section organization remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 removes bold emphasis from parts of the abstract and changes text flow and page breaks, including extending the conclusion onto page 9. Figures 1–5 and Tables 1–10 retain their displays and captions; appendix pages 13–17 are visually identical.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly improves scholarly presentation through more complete publication details and page ranges in the references, cleaner bibliographic formatting, and explicit funding disclosure. The scientific argument, experimental evidence, and reproducibility information are unchanged, so the benefit is limited to editorial completeness and traceability.
